title: Self-Employed? Roth is One of Four Accounts
subtitle: If you work for yourself, you have four retirement accounts to choose from. Only one is Roth-by-default. Here's the order to fund them.
source_irs: IRC §401(k) (Solo 401k); IRC §408(k) (SIMPLE IRA); IRC §408(p) (SEP IRA); IRC §219 (Roth IRA)

concepts.heading: The Four Accounts
concepts.lede: Self-employed people get four accounts. Three are pre-tax (with a Roth option), one is Roth-only.
body: 1. Solo 401(k) — up to $72,000/yr (2025 §415(c) limit). Has employee deferral + employer profit-sharing + after-tax.
2. SEP IRA — up to ~25% of net self-employment income, max ~$70,000. Pre-tax only.
3. SIMPLE IRA — up to ~$16,500 (2026). Pre-tax or Roth option since 2023.
4. Roth IRA — $7,500. Income phaseout at $153K-$168K single.

concepts.heading: The Funding Order
concepts.lede: Solo 401(k) employee deferral is the cornerstone. Then the Roth IRA. Then the employer-side match/profit-sharing as Roth.
body: Step 1: Solo 401(k) employee deferral, $24,500 (2026), pre-tax OR Roth.
Step 3: Solo 401(k) employer profit-sharing, up to 25% of net SE income. Pre-tax by default, but can designate as Roth if the plan allows.
Step 4: SEP IRA as backup if no Solo 401(k) (simpler admin, lower limit).

concepts.heading: The Trap
concepts.lede: Most self-employed people only use SEP IRA. They leave 30-50% of their retirement tax shelter on the table.
body: SEP IRA contribution = ~$70,000 max, but ALL pre-tax.
The $24,500 employee deferral has the Roth option. SEP does not.
If you skip the Solo 401(k), you skip the Roth mega-backdoor and the Roth deferral. That's a 6-figure tax loss over 30 years.
